title.text: Matt Pocock Skills: Daily Developer Guide
picker.label: Language
hero.title: How to use these skills in actual daily dev work
hero.intro1: This guide is not a repo summary. It is a practical operating manual for using the skills as a software developer: shaping a feature, fixing a bug, spinning up a prototype, writing tests, understanding an unfamiliar codebase, and keeping work ready for async agent execution.
hero.intro2: Core frame: treat the agent as a junior engineer with weird constraints, not smart autocomplete. The skills encode the senior-engineer habits that keep that junior productive — slow down, build context, write one test at a time, then zoom back out.
hero.flow3: Use the workflow recipe that matches your task.
hero.flow4: Prefer small vertical slices over big all-at-once implementation.
toc.heading: Use Cases
mentalModel.heading: Mental Model
mentalModel.prototype.html: Prototype: answer a question with throwaway code.
mentalModel.prdIssues.html: Spec / Tickets: turn decisions into executable work.
mentalModel.tddDiagnose.html: TDD / Diagnose: use feedback loops instead of guessing.
mentalModel.implement.html: Implement: execute slices end to end, one issue at a time.
caveats.heading: Caveats
caveats.stackBias.html: Integration bias: setup supports GitHub, Linear, and local files; custom trackers need their own adapter. Several misc utilities are JS/TS-specific.
caveats.modelStrength.html: Model strength: grilling skills can bail or refuse on smaller / non-frontier models. Use Claude or GPT frontier tiers for best results.
caveats.installLean.html: Install lean: only enable the skills you'll actually use. A bloated skill set hurts the agent's intent matching.
start.heading: Start Here
start.intro: The repo is designed around small composable skills, but there is still one setup step you should not skip.
start.install.heading: 1. Install
start.install.body.html: Choose managed Claude Code plugin or editable skills.sh files. Do not install both. With skills.sh, include /setup-matt-pocock-skills.
start.configure.heading: 2. Configure Per Repo
start.configure.body.html: Run /setup-matt-pocock-skills once. It records your issue tracker, triage labels, and whether the repo has one global domain context or multiple.
start.callout1: If you skip setup, the planning and issue skills lose context about where tickets live and how the repo documents domain language and architecture.
start.callout2.html: Pick one install path. Claude Code plugin is a managed, read-only subscription that updates with upstream. skills.sh copies editable files you own. Installing both gives you every skill twice.
start.install1.heading.html: Option A · Claude Code plugin managed + auto-updated
start.install1.intro.html: Install official marketplace plugin. Files stay read-only; updates arrive when Matt ships them.
start.install2.heading.html: Option B · Codex + other agents editable local files
start.install2.intro: Use skills.sh. Choose desired skills and include /setup-matt-pocock-skills. Update later with npx skills update.
start.install2.label: Run in your shell
feature.heading: New Feature
feature.intro: Best when you want disciplined delivery instead of “build everything from a vague prompt”.
feature.step1.html: 1. Stress-test the idea: use /grill-with-docs so the agent asks one question at a time and reconciles your plan with existing repo language in CONTEXT.md and ADRs.
feature.step2.html: 2. Freeze the shape: use /to-spec to synthesize the current conversation into a buildable spec without another interview.
feature.step3.html: 3. Break into slices: use /to-tickets so implementation tickets are thin vertical slices, not “backend first, frontend later” horizontal chunks.
feature.step4.html: 4. Build safely: use /implement to execute the first unblocked ticket — it uses TDD internally, one observable behavior at a time through public interfaces.
feature.callout: Expect grilling to be substantial — 15–40 questions is normal, not a quick chat. That is the point: the agent surfaces every decision you would otherwise hit during coding, where it costs ten times more to fix.
feature.whyBody: The pack tries to eliminate the two common failures: unclear feature intent and giant speculative implementation. It forces decisions to solidify before coding.
feature.ruleBody.html: /implement uses TDD internally and explicitly rejects horizontal slicing. Do not write all tests first and all code second. Do one test, one implementation, repeat.
bug.heading: Bug Fix
bug.intro: Use this when a defect is real but the cause is still unclear, or when you need a repeatable regression test before claiming the fix.
bug.step1.html: 1. Prime the context: read CONTEXT.md and any ADRs in the area before diving in. If the codebase is a blank slate, skim the relevant module files directly.
bug.step2.html: 2. Build a feedback loop: describe the bug to the agent — it will invoke the diagnosing-bugs skill automatically. Its core rule: do not guess before you have a reproducible pass/fail loop.
bug.step3.html: 3. Rank hypotheses: the skill pushes the agent to generate several falsifiable hypotheses before changing code.
bug.step4.html: 4. Fix and lock it down: once the root cause is confirmed, turn the minimized repro into a failing regression test. The agent uses the tdd loop to implement the repair, one behavior at a time.
bug.callout.html: The strongest idea in diagnosing-bugs: a fast deterministic loop is 90% of the bug fix. No loop, no serious debugging.
project.heading: Craft A New Project
project.intro: There is no single “new project” skill here. The repo expects you to compose a project workflow from planning, prototype, and delivery skills.
project.bestChain.html: Best chain grill-me → prototype → to-spec → to-tickets → implement per ticket
project.step1.html: 1. Clarify the product: use /grill-me if you want a relentless interview without repo-document updates yet.
project.step2.html: 2. Prove the risky idea: use /prototype to answer the hardest question first, either logic/state or UI direction.
project.step3.html: 3. Turn it into an artifact: use /to-spec once the concept stops moving.
project.step4.html: 4. Turn strategy into slices: use /to-tickets so the first build steps are independently shippable.
project.step5.html: 5. Build one ticket at a time: take the first unblocked slice and implement it with /implement, which uses TDD at pre-agreed seams.
project.step6.html: 6. Repeat until the project exists: close each ticket, pick the next slice, and use /handoff between sessions if another agent or future-you needs to continue.
project.whenGrillMeBody.html: Use it before code exists, or when you want pure design pressure-testing without touching CONTEXT.md and ADRs yet.
project.whenGrillDocsBody: Use it once a repo exists and your terminology should align with the existing domain language and documented architectural choices.
project.callout.html: Important: /to-tickets is not the end of the project. It is the handoff from planning into execution. After that: pick one ticket, implement it with /implement, close it, then move to the next unblocked slice.
huge.heading: Huge / Foggy Project
huge.intro: Use this only when the destination cannot fit inside one sharp session: major migration, greenfield platform, or multi-team rewrite with unknowns behind unknowns.
huge.step1.html: 1. Name destination: /wayfinder first defines what “done planning” means.
huge.step2.html: 2. Chart visible frontier: create decision tickets for questions sharp enough to ask; leave everything else under fog of war.
huge.step3.html: 3. Resolve one decision per session: research, prototype, grill, or complete a human/agent task. Closed decisions reveal new frontier tickets.
huge.step4.html: 4. Collapse map into delivery: once route is clear, use /to-spec, /to-tickets, then fresh /implement sessions per unblocked ticket.
huge.callout.html: Do not use Wayfinder for a well-scoped feature. It maps decisions, not build tasks. Going straight from map to /implement discards linked reasoning.
legacy.heading: Legacy / Unfamiliar Codebase
legacy.intro: New job, inherited service, or a repo that grew faster than its docs? Do not apply the greenfield flow. The agent cannot respect architecture that only lives in your head.
legacy.step1.html: 1. Survey the terrain: run /improve-codebase-architecture to surface the muddiest seams and the highest-leverage deepening opportunities. You are not refactoring yet — you are forming a map.
legacy.step2.html: 2. Seed the shared language: use /grill-with-docs to create or extend CONTEXT.md. Capture domain terms now, before the agent has to invent them on the fly.
legacy.step3.html: 3. Read before you touch: before changing a specific module, read it directly — using CONTEXT.md and ADRs as your map — so the change lands with full awareness of callers and boundaries.
legacy.step4.html: 4. Resume normal flow: once context exists, switch into the feature or bug recipe. The setup pays back across every subsequent session.
legacy.callout.html: Skipping straight to /implement in a legacy codebase produces code that fits the agent's guess of the system, not the system itself. Establish context first.
poc.heading: PoC / Prototype
poc.intro: This is one of the repo's clearest and most useful skills. Prototype code is meant to answer a question, not quietly become production code.
poc.logicBody: Use when the question is: “does this state machine, workflow, or domain model behave correctly?” Build a tiny interactive terminal app.
poc.uiBody: Use when the question is: “what should this look like?” Build multiple radically different variants on one route, switchable by URL param.
poc.rulesBody: One command to run. No persistence by default. Minimal polish. Surface the full state after each action. Delete or absorb the result when the question is answered.
testing.heading: Testing
testing.intro: The repo's testing posture is strongly behavior-first. It prefers tests that survive refactors because they verify public behavior, not private structure.
testing.check2: Tests should describe what the system does, not how internals are wired.
testing.check3: Good tests are usually integration-style and survive internal refactors.
testing.check4: Each red-green cycle should cover one behavior only.
testing.check5: Refactor only when the suite is green.
testing.useForBody: New behavior, bug fixes with a clear seam, and any change where you want a disciplined red-green-refactor loop.
testing.avoidBody.html: Mock-heavy tests tied to internal collaborators, private methods, or internal call graphs. If renaming internals breaks tests, the tests are too coupled. And resist bulk-writing tests up front — that verifies imagined behavior, not observed behavior. Let each test discover the next one.
quickdev.heading: Quick Dev
quickdev.intro: Use a lighter chain when you need speed, but keep the right guardrails depending on whether the task is ambiguity, direction, or verbosity.
quickdev.routerBody.html: Use /ask-matt — it routes you to the right skill or flow based on your situation.
quickdev.promptingBody.html: Use /grill-me for a short pre-implementation interview when the plan is fuzzy.
quickdev.tokensBody.html: Use /caveman (external skill — see install below) for terse but technically accurate responses.
quickdev.cavemanCallout.html: /caveman is now a separate community skill. Install it once across your agents: npx skills@latest add JuliusBrussee/caveman
maintenance.heading: Codebase Maintenance
maintenance.intro: This repo is not only about shipping features. It also assumes agent-assisted development can accelerate codebase entropy if you never zoom back out.
maintenance.step1.html: Improve architecture: run /improve-codebase-architecture every few days to look for deeper modules and places where the system is turning into a ball of mud.
maintenance.step2.html: Feed your CONTEXT.md: revisit it whenever new terms, modules, or decisions land. Treat it as a living glossary, not a one-time export.
maintenance.step3.html: Triage incoming work: use /triage if your workflow depends on issue states like needs-triage, ready-for-agent, and wontfix.
maintenance.step4.html: Stop losing context: use /handoff when another session or another agent needs to continue the work cleanly.
maintenance.callout1.html: Context decay is real: skip a week of edits to CONTEXT.md and ADRs and the agent's accuracy regresses fast. The shared language is only powerful while it stays current with the code.
maintenance.callout2: Good daily use is less about memorizing every skill and more about learning a few stable chains you can reuse: clarify, slice, build, verify, then zoom back out.
recipes.heading: Recommended Recipes
recipes.intro: Use these as defaults until you form your own habits.
recipes.unsureBody.html: /ask-matt — routes you to the right flow.
recipes.uiBody.html: /prototype with multiple variants on one route.
recipes.wizardBody.html: Ask for setup/cutover → wizard generates guided bash flow.
recipes.pairingBody.html: /caveman (external — install from JuliusBrussee/caveman) while keeping the rest of your workflow unchanged.
mistakes.heading: Common Mistakes
mistakes.intro: These skills are opinionated. They are strongest when you obey the intended constraints.
mistakes.item1.html: Do not skip /setup-matt-pocock-skills and then expect issue-based workflows to behave correctly.
mistakes.item2.html: Do not use /implement as “write a full test suite, then fill in implementation later”.
mistakes.item3.html: Do not let diagnosing-bugs become an excuse to brainstorm without a reproducible loop.
mistakes.item4: Do not let prototype code quietly become production without either deletion or a deliberate absorption step.
mistakes.item5.html: Do not use /grill-with-docs without caring about domain language and ADRs. That is the point of the skill.
sim.heading: Simulated Sessions
sim.intro: These are the examples the earlier prompts were missing: realistic flows from the first user message to a solved outcome, including when the skill chain switches.
sim.bug.heading: Bug Fix: Checkout Timeout
sim.bug.user.html: Customers sometimes hit a timeout on checkout after entering a promo code. Diagnose the root cause — build a reproducible loop, rank the hypotheses, and instrument the system before touching code. Once you confirm the cause, add a failing regression test and fix it, keeping the change minimal.
sim.bug.agent1.html: It reads CONTEXT.md and the checkout module, builds the fastest reproducible loop, then the diagnosing-bugs skill ranks hypotheses: retry storms, stale pricing cache, or promo validation deadlock.
sim.bug.agent2.html: After instrumentation, it proves the timeout happens when promo validation calls pricing twice under one request. The tdd skill then writes the failing regression test around checkout with a promo code, applies the smallest fix, and reruns the suite.
sim.bug.done: You get a root-cause explanation, the regression test, the code fix, and confirmation that the deterministic repro loop now passes.
sim.feature.heading: New Feature: Saved Drafts
sim.feature.user.html: We need saved drafts for long support replies. Use /grill-with-docs to challenge the idea against existing inbox rules. When the shape is clear, run /to-spec, then /to-tickets, then build the first unblocked slice with /implement.
sim.feature.agent1: It asks one question at a time: per-user or shared drafts, autosave timing, conflict behavior, retention, and whether drafts belong to threads or replies. It checks existing domain docs and ADRs before asking questions already answered in the repo.
sim.feature.agent2.html: Once the decisions stop moving, /to-spec turns the conversation into a stable artifact. /to-tickets then slices the work into vertical units such as draft persistence, editor restore, and draft conflict handling. The first slice is implemented via /implement.
sim.feature.done: You end with a clarified feature, a spec, actionable tickets, and one shipped slice backed by behavior-first tests.
sim.poc.heading: PoC: New Onboarding Flow
sim.poc.user.html: We are unsure whether onboarding should feel like a wizard or a checklist. Use /prototype to create two radically different UI variants on one route. Keep it throwaway and capture the decision signal we learn from it.
sim.poc.agent1.html: /prototype chooses the UI branch, creates multiple variants, and makes them easy to switch between with a URL parameter. It keeps persistence and polish minimal because the goal is comparison, not production readiness.
sim.poc.agent2: After review, it summarizes the tradeoff: for example, the wizard reduces cognitive load for new users, while the checklist makes progress resumable and transparent. It records which variant won and why.
sim.poc.done: You get a decision, not just a mockup. Keep the prototype as a primary source on its branch, then convert the chosen direction into a spec and tickets.
sim.greenfield.heading: Greenfield Project: Internal Tool
sim.greenfield.user.html: I want an internal approvals dashboard, but the scope is fuzzy. Start with /grill-me. When we know the riskiest assumption, use /prototype. If the concept holds up, create the spec and tickets.
sim.greenfield.agent1.html: /grill-me narrows the problem: approver roles, SLA expectations, queue size, escalation, and reporting needs. It recommends answers and challenges weak assumptions one branch at a time.
sim.greenfield.agent2.html: It identifies the riskiest assumption as queue triage usability, so /prototype builds a minimal interaction model first. If the model works, /to-spec and /to-tickets convert the idea into a buildable roadmap.
sim.greenfield.agent3.html: Then execution begins: it picks the first unblocked ticket, uses /implement to execute that vertical slice with TDD, closes it, and repeats slice by slice until the approvals dashboard works end to end.
sim.greenfield.done: You move from fuzzy idea to validated direction to implementable slices, then to a real working project built one issue at a time.
skills.heading: All Skills In Detail
skills.intro: Every current skill in the repository, grouped by category. This section is for the “what exactly does this one do?” question, not just which workflow to chain.
skills.engineering.heading: Engineering Skills
skills.engineering.intro: Core execution skills for planning, implementation, debugging, issue slicing, and architecture work. Skills marked model-invoked activate automatically when you describe your intent — you don't need to type the slash command explicitly.
skills.productivity.heading: Productivity Skills
skills.productivity.intro: Conversation-shaping skills for clarification, continuity, async decisions, agent-facing writing, and structured learning.
skills.external.heading: External / Community Skills
skills.external.intro: Skills not in the mattpocock/skills pack — installed separately. Install with npx skills@latest add <repo>.
skills.misc.heading: Misc Skills
skills.misc.intro: Specialized utilities for setup, migration, exercise scaffolding, and defensive tooling.
skills.askMatt.useWhen.html: Use when: you're not sure which skill or flow fits your current situation.
skills.askMatt.what.html: What it does: acts as a router over all user-invoked skills — describes the main flow, the on-ramps, and the standalone skills, then recommends the right path.
skills.askMatt.constraint.html: Constraint: start here when you're stuck, not when you already know the chain.
skills.setup.useWhen.html: Use when: setting up a repo for the first time.
skills.setup.what.html: What it does: configures issue-tracker integration, label mapping, and how domain documentation is organized so the other skills have context.
skills.setup.constraint.html: Constraint: this is the prerequisite skill; the planning and triage skills depend on it.
skills.grillDocs.useWhen.html: Use when: shaping a feature in an existing repo where ADRs and domain docs matter.
skills.grillDocs.what.html: What it does: asks one question at a time, checks the repo first so it does not re-ask anything already answered in CONTEXT.md or ADRs, then writes new decisions back into those docs. Proposes ADRs only for major calls.
skills.grillDocs.constraint.html: Constraint: this is for repo-aware planning, not casual ideation.
skills.toPrd.useWhen.html: Use when: the conversation is mature enough to be frozen into a spec.
skills.toPrd.what.html: What it does: synthesizes discussion into a tracker-published spec without re-interviewing you.
skills.toPrd.constraint.html: Constraint: it prefers durable intent over code-level implementation trivia.
skills.toIssues.useWhen.html: Use when: you need execution-ready tickets from a spec or design conversation.
skills.toIssues.what.html: What it does: creates tracer-bullet vertical slices and explicit blocking edges.
skills.toIssues.constraint.html: Constraint: it rejects horizontal slicing as the default breakdown.
skills.implement.useWhen.html: Use when: you have a spec or set of tickets and want the agent to execute them end to end.
skills.implement.what.html: What it does: works through the described work using TDD at pre-agreed seams, runs typechecking regularly, and runs /code-review before committing.
skills.implement.constraint.html: Constraint: best used after planning is complete — not as a shortcut past design.
skills.diagnosingBugs.useWhen.html: Use when: a bug is real but the cause is unknown — just describe the problem and the agent applies this skill automatically.
skills.diagnosingBugs.what.html: What it does: builds a tight reproducible loop, ranks falsifiable hypotheses, instruments the system, verifies the root cause, then locks the fix with a regression test.
skills.diagnosingBugs.constraint.html: Constraint: no serious debugging without a loop you trust.
skills.prototype.useWhen.html: Use when: you need to answer a question quickly with throwaway code.
skills.prototype.what.html: What it does: branches into logic prototypes or multi-variant UI prototypes, optimized for learning rather than polish.
skills.prototype.constraint.html: Constraint: prototype output should be deleted or deliberately absorbed later.
skills.triage.useWhen.html: Use when: sorting incoming issues or preparing them for async agent execution.
skills.triage.what.html: What it does: applies a state machine to labels, reproduces when possible, and writes structured issue comments for maintainers or agents.
skills.triage.constraint.html: Constraint: relies on the label conventions configured during setup.
skills.improveArch.useWhen.html: Use when: the repo is getting shallow, scattered, or harder to reason about.
skills.improveArch.what.html: What it does: searches for high-leverage refactors that deepen modules and improve locality while staying aligned with repo vocabulary and ADRs.
skills.improveArch.constraint.html: Constraint: it starts by identifying candidate opportunities, not by inventing abstractions in the abstract.
skills.wayfinder.useWhen.html: Use when: a project or migration is too large and foggy for one context window.
skills.wayfinder.what.html: What it does: maps decision tickets, blocking edges, and fog of war; resolves one decision per session until a buildable route appears.
skills.wayfinder.constraint.html: Constraint: it produces decisions, not deliverables; finish with /to-spec.
skills.tdd.useWhen.html: Use when: building concrete behavior test-first, alone or inside /implement.
skills.tdd.what.html: What it does: runs one vertical red-green-refactor slice at a time through public seams.
skills.tdd.constraint.html: Constraint: never write all tests first; each passing slice discovers the next.
skills.codeReview.useWhen.html: Use when: reviewing a branch, PR, or WIP diff since a fixed point.
skills.codeReview.what.html: What it does: runs Standards and Spec reviews in parallel, then reports both axes side by side.
skills.codeReview.constraint.html: Constraint: give it a real base commit, branch, tag, or merge-base.
skills.research.useWhen.html: Use when: a decision needs current facts from primary sources.
skills.research.what.html: What it does: delegates reading to a background agent and saves a cited Markdown brief in repo.
skills.research.constraint.html: Constraint: research feeds planning; it does not replace /grill-with-docs.
skills.mergeConflicts.useWhen.html: Use when: a merge or rebase is already stopped on conflicts.
skills.mergeConflicts.what.html: What it does: resolves each hunk by intent traced to both sides' primary sources, then finishes Git.
skills.mergeConflicts.constraint.html: Constraint: it never chooses ours/theirs blindly and never aborts the operation.
skills.wizard.useWhen.html: Use when: setup needs human-only browser, credential, secret, migration, or cutover steps.
skills.wizard.what.html: What it does: generates a verified bash wizard that opens URLs, captures values, and writes env or CI secrets stage by stage.
skills.wizard.constraint.html: Constraint: only for steps the agent genuinely cannot perform itself.
skills.grillMe.useWhen.html: Use when: an idea is fuzzy and you want a direct interview without the repo-document coupling of /grill-with-docs.
skills.grillMe.what.html: What it does: asks one question at a time, recommends an answer with each question, and resolves uncertainty aggressively.
skills.grillMe.constraint.html: Constraint: this is the generic planning interrogator, not the repo-aware one.
skills.handoff.useWhen.html: Use when: another session or agent must continue the work.
skills.handoff.what.html: What it does: writes a compact handoff summary to a temp file, references existing artifacts, and recommends next-step skills.
skills.handoff.constraint.html: Constraint: it is meant to minimize duplication, not create another giant document.
skills.questionnaire.useWhen.html: Use when: a decision is blocked by facts or preferences held by someone else.
skills.questionnaire.what.html: What it does: grills you about the send, then writes a focused Markdown questionnaire for that person to answer asynchronously.
skills.questionnaire.constraint.html: Constraint: questions target the missing decision input, not generic discovery.
skills.waitWhat.useWhen.html: Use when: the agent's last message did not land.
skills.waitWhat.what.html: What it does: re-pitches the same point in plain English with missing context and repo vocabulary.
skills.waitWhat.constraint.html: Constraint: corrective, not a substitute for building shared language up front.
skills.teach.useWhen.html: Use when: you want to learn a topic progressively across multiple sessions in a dedicated workspace.
skills.teach.what.html: What it does: treats the working directory as a teaching workspace, capturing a MISSION.md, curated resources, learning records, and beautiful self-contained HTML lessons that target your zone of proximal development.
skills.teach.constraint.html: Constraint: stateful — relies on the workspace files surviving between sessions, and never trusts the agent's parametric knowledge over cited resources.
skills.writingGreatSkills.useWhen.html: Use when: creating or editing a skill, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, or any doc an agent reaches through a pointer.
skills.writingGreatSkills.what.html: What it does: makes agent-facing docs scannable, explicit, and progressively disclosed.
skills.writingGreatSkills.constraint.htm: Constraint: optimize for agent retrieval and action, not essay-style reading.
skills.grilling.useWhen.html: Use when: another workflow needs its reusable one-question-at-a-time interview primitive.
skills.grilling.what.html: What it does: separates facts the agent can discover from decisions only the user can make.
skills.grilling.constraint.html: Constraint: normally invoked under grill, triage, wayfinder, or architecture flows.
skills.domainModeling.useWhen.html: Use when: pinning down domain terminology, recording an architectural decision, or building the ubiquitous language for the project.
skills.domainModeling.what.html: What it does: actively builds and sharpens the domain model — challenges terms, invents edge-case scenarios, and writes the glossary and decisions into CONTEXT.md and ADRs as they crystallise.
skills.domainModeling.constraint.html: Constraint: for changing the model, not just reading it.
skills.codebaseDesign.useWhen.html: Use when: designing or improving a module's interface, deciding where a seam goes, or making code more testable and AI-navigable.
skills.codebaseDesign.what.html: What it does: provides shared vocabulary for designing deep modules — a lot of behaviour behind a small interface, placed at a clean seam.
skills.codebaseDesign.constraint.html: Constraint: uses specific terminology (module, seam, interface) — don’t substitute “component” or “service”.
skills.cavemanExt.useWhen.html: Use when: you want low-token, terse responses during pairing or rapid iteration.
skills.cavemanExt.what.html: What it does: ~65% output token reduction across multiple compression levels. Drops filler words and articles while preserving full technical accuracy. Persists until disabled.
skills.gitGuardrails.useWhen.html: Use when: you want Claude Code protected from destructive git commands.
skills.gitGuardrails.what.html: What it does: installs hooks that block risky commands such as force pushes, hard resets, aggressive cleans, and destructive branch deletion.
skills.gitGuardrails.constraint.html: Constraint: geared specifically toward Claude Code hook-based workflows.
skills.migrateShoehorn.useWhen.html: Use when: test code contains too many ugly TypeScript assertions.
skills.migrateShoehorn.what.html: What it does: migrates tests to @total-typescript/shoehorn helpers like fromPartial() and fromAny().
skills.migrateShoehorn.constraint.html: Constraint: it is for test code, not production code.
skills.scaffoldExercises.useWhen.html: Use when: you are building workshop or course exercises with consistent folder conventions.
skills.scaffoldExercises.what.html: What it does: scaffolds numbered exercise structures and iterates until the exercise linter passes.
skills.scaffoldExercises.constraint.html: Constraint: useful mainly for repos that already follow this training-content layout.
skills.setupPreCommit.useWhen.html: Use when: a JS/TS repo needs commit-time formatting and safety checks.
skills.setupPreCommit.what.html: What it does: wires Husky, lint-staged, and Prettier into a pre-commit workflow, adapting to the package manager it finds.
skills.setupPreCommit.constraint.html: Constraint: it uses only scripts that already exist instead of inventing missing test or typecheck commands.
footer.sources.html: Source material: mattpocock/skills@6654f6b (2026-08-24), its current reference, and JuliusBrussee/caveman.
